On the first Monday of every month, the railway sold its unclaimed umbrellas. It sold the black ones for two dollars and the colored ones for three, because Mr. Vale, who ran the lost-property office, believed that anyone willing to carry a yellow umbrella ought to be charged for the pleasure.

Everything else went to auction twice a year. There were always more shoes than seemed reasonable. A person might leave a train without a hat, but how did they leave without a shoe? Mr. Vale had been asking this question for twenty-seven years. His assistant, Nina, once suggested that the answer was probably different for every shoe. He found this unsatisfying.

One Tuesday in November, a conductor brought in a kitchen chair.

“Carriage four,” she said.

“How did they get it on?”

“The doors open.”

“How did they forget it?”

The conductor shrugged. “Same way you forgot my birthday.”

Mr. Vale wrote *one chair, wooden, green*, on a tag, tied it to a rung, and wished the conductor a happy birthday. It turned out her birthday was in April. What annoyed her was that he hadn’t known enough to object.

The chair had a rush seat and one short leg. Nina slid a folded timetable under it and began eating her lunch there. From that angle she could see a slice of platform through the office window, low enough that passengers passed as a succession of shoes. On Friday she watched two pairs stop, turn toward each other, and remain still long after the train had gone. One person had a hole in the sole. She could see it each time he lifted his heel.

After three weeks, a boy came in and asked for the chair.

“Can you describe it?” said Mr. Vale.

“It’s uncomfortable.”

“Anything else?”

“Green. There’s a burn underneath.”

Nina tipped the chair over. There was indeed a dark oval on the underside of the seat.

“How do you burn the bottom of a chair?” she asked.

“With a toaster,” said the boy, and offered nothing further.

Mr. Vale unfastened the tag. The boy made no move to take the chair.

“Can I leave it here till four?”

“You’ve left it here since the seventh. I suppose we can manage another hour.”

At four, the boy returned with a woman wearing slippers inside plastic grocery bags. She walked slowly but refused his arm. At the sight of the chair she said, “Oh, you idiot,” and sat down.

The boy crouched to adjust the timetable under the short leg.

“It was on the train,” he told her.

“I know where it was. I put it there.”

This was the first Mr. Vale had heard of anybody putting a thing on a train without intending to take it off again. He lowered the lid of his lunch tin very quietly.

The woman had been moving out of a house. Her son had hired a van, and the men kept asking what was coming and what was going. She had put the chair on the pavement to sit on while she decided. Then the van went, her son went, and she took the chair to the station. She had bought it forty years earlier from a café that was closing down. It had cost less than her sandwich.

“I thought if I left it somewhere, I wouldn’t have to tell anybody they could throw it away,” she said.

“You could have told me,” the boy said.

“You’d have brought it back.”

He looked down at his hands, which were still on the chair leg.

Mr. Vale asked whether they would like him to put the tag back on. The woman considered this. Outside, an announcement began halfway through a sentence and gave up before naming the station.

“Do you need a chair?” she asked Nina.

“I have one at the desk.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

Nina looked at the chair behind her desk. It had wheels and could be raised or lowered by a lever. Nobody had ever asked if she needed it.

“Yes,” she said.

The woman got up. The boy took her arm this time, and they went out together. Visible through the window, the grocery bags made her feet look enormous. The boy had to shorten his stride so much he was almost walking in place.

The following morning, Nina found the folded timetable on her desk. Mr. Vale had sawed a thin round of wood from the end of a broom handle and glued it to the short leg. He had painted the new foot green. It was not quite the right green, and he had turned the chair to face the wall while it dried, as though it had done something wrong.

They kept it by the window. People trying to describe their missing things often sat in it. From time to time they surprised themselves by remembering a detail: a telephone number written inside a glove, or a set of keys with a little screwdriver attached. One man, who had come in about a briefcase, sat for ten minutes and then said it might be at home. It was. He called to tell them, and Mr. Vale, who had no place on his form for a briefcase that had never been missing, took down the message anyway.

In spring, the conductor brought in a single brown shoe. It was scuffed at the toe, with a new blue lace threaded through only the top two holes. Mr. Vale turned it over. There was nothing remarkable about the sole.

“Well?” said Nina.

He put the shoe on the shelf.

A week later, someone came for it. She was a woman in work trousers, out of breath from crossing the footbridge. She described the lace before Mr. Vale could ask. Then she sat in the green chair and took an identical shoe out of her bag. She set them side by side on her knees and pressed each toe with her thumb.

Mr. Vale was about to ask how she’d lost it. He had the words ready. But the woman was smiling down at the shoes, and after a moment he went back to counting the umbrellas.
